title: Best specialist lap
explain: The specialist has driven only this one track during training, so it knows every corner. Watch it accelerate hard from the start, hold high speed on the straights, keep its speed through the bends by staying close to the edge, and take the jump without slowing down. It is the fastest of all drivers evaluated so far on this track, but what it learned is how to drive this one track: on tracks with a different layout it mostly falls off (see the results).

title: Best generalist lap on a hand-made track it never saw in training: it generalized
explain: This is generalization: driving well on a track the model never saw in training. The generalist learned on tens of thousands of generated tracks and never on these hand-made ones, which were designed separately. It reads the road ahead, picks a speed for each bend, and laps this track in about half the scripted driver's time. On the specialist's own track it is only slightly slower than the specialist (see the results). Compare clip 7 among the negative results: the specialist on this same track.
why: the highest-scoring finished track of the 5 campaign tracks it finished

title: Best generalist lap on a held-out generated track it never saw in training: it generalized
explain: Generalization again, now on a generated track from the held-out test seeds: the same kind of track as in training, but never this one, driven from the standing start to the finish. Watch it slow down for each bend, hug the inside edge through it and accelerate out again, using only what it sees of the road ahead. Compare it with the next clip, the scripted driver on the same track.
why: the highest-scoring finished track of the 779 test tracks it finished

title: Scripted driver on the same held-out track, for comparison
explain: The same track as the clip before, driven by the hand-written scripted driver. It drives the track cleanly, but it is cautious: in the bends it slows to well under half the generalist's speed, and it never reaches the speeds the generalist holds on the straights, so it needs almost twice as long (speeds measured from both recorded runs). Its time on each track is the yardstick of the score: 1.0 means as fast as this driver.
why: the same track as the generalist/seed0 clip: the highest-scoring finished track of the 779 test tracks `generalist/seed0` finished

title: Seed 1's specialist finishes a held-out track it never trained on: it generalized
explain: This is generalization too, by a specialist: driving well on a track it never saw in training. It is a second specialist, trained the same way on campaign track 1 only but with seed 1. It finishes about one unseen test track in five, and this is a typical one of them (median score). Its finishes lean towards easier tracks like this one: shorter, less banked and with fewer jumps than average. Where its driving carries over it is fast: on the tracks both finish it is as fast as the generalist, slightly faster on most of them, and on this track the two times are almost equal (see the evaluation line). But the generalist also finishes almost all of the tracks the specialist finishes, plus many harder ones the specialist falls off: about four unseen test tracks in five. That is the difference between learning one track and learning many.
why: the median-scoring finished track of the 192 test tracks it finished

title: The specialist does not generalize: clip 1's model on clip 2's track, which it never trained on
explain: The specialist from clip 1, on the track of clip 2, which it never trained on. For the first seconds it accelerates exactly like the generalist, but then it brakes to a crawl, drifts towards the edge of a bend and drops off the road, while the generalist on the same track keeps accelerating (clip 2; speeds compared from both recorded runs). Trained on one track, it learned to drive that track, and that driving does not carry over to a different layout, which is why the README's results show it finishing so few unseen tracks.
why: the same track as the generalist/seed0 clip: the highest-scoring finished track of the 5 campaign tracks `generalist/seed0` finished

title: Generalization failure on a held-out track: the generalist falls off halfway round
explain: Generalization does not always work. About one unseen track in five ends like this: the generalist enters a bend too fast, cannot hold the line and leaves the road on the outside. Most of its falls come right after tight corners rather than at jumps (failure analysis in `results/generalist/seed*/failures_*.json`): it trades safety for speed.
why: the fall whose position is closest to the middle of its track among its 190 falls on test tracks

title: Generalization failure beyond the training range: a corner tighter than any training track
explain: This track was generated with tighter corners than any track the generalist trained on. It approaches the corner at a speed that would suit the wider corners it knows and flies off the outside. Learning from many tracks lets it drive new combinations of familiar features, but not features outside what it has seen: on tracks like this it almost always falls, while longer jumps than in training, for example, are handled well (see the results).
why: the fall whose position is closest to the middle of its track among its 43 falls on tight-turn out-of-range tracks

title: Untrained network (control) on the specialist's track
explain: Like every evaluated driver, the network takes its most probable action at each step instead of sampling one. With random initial weights its output layer starts close to zero (standard deviation 0.01, the CleanRL convention), so it picks almost the same keys every step, here steering right while coasting, and never presses gas. Sampled instead of taken greedily, the same network would press keys almost uniformly at random, which is how PPO starts exploring.

caption.What you see: Like every evaluated driver, the network takes its most probable action at each step instead of sampling one. With random initial weights its output layer starts close to zero (standard deviation 0.01, the CleanRL convention), so it picks almost the same keys every step, here steering right while coasting, and never presses gas. Sampled instead of taken greedily, the same network would press keys almost uniformly at random, which is how PPO starts exploring.
caption.Model: `baselines/untrained/seed0`: the same network as the trained agents (2 × 256 units) with random initial weights (seed 0) and no training; a control.
caption.Map: First Flight (`campaign-01`), a hand-made campaign track, 628 m long with 1 jump and up to 6° of banking; this network was never trained on any track.
caption.Evaluation: official evaluation in `results/baselines/untrained/seed0/eval_campaign.csv` (standing start, most probable action, final checkpoint): did not finish: stalled after 2.00 s and 6 m (the scripted driver finishes in 30.17 s). The clip replays this run.

title: Untrained network with sampled actions: almost uniformly random keys, as PPO starts exploring
explain: The same network and weights as the clip before. The official evaluation takes the most probable action; here the keys of every step are drawn from the network's own probabilities, which are close to one in three for each steering and each pedal choice, so they are almost uniformly random, as at the start of PPO training. The car jitters between gas, coast and brake and drifts a few dozen metres before it is out for lack of progress. This is a demonstration run, not part of the scored evaluation.

caption.What you see: The same network and weights as the clip before. The official evaluation takes the most probable action; here the keys of every step are drawn from the network's own probabilities, which are close to one in three for each steering and each pedal choice, so they are almost uniformly random, as at the start of PPO training. The car jitters between gas, coast and brake and drifts a few dozen metres before it is out for lack of progress. This is a demonstration run, not part of the scored evaluation.
caption.Model: `demos/untrained-sampled/seed0`: the untrained control network (random initial weights, seed 0) with each action sampled from its probabilities (sampling seed 1000) instead of the most probable one.
caption.Map: First Flight (`campaign-01`), a hand-made campaign track, 628 m long with 1 jump and up to 6° of banking; this network was never trained on any track.
caption.Evaluation: demonstration run through the same evaluator, recorded in `results/demos/untrained-sampled/seed0/eval_campaign.csv` (standing start, sampled actions; not scored): did not finish: stalled after 28.99 s and 52 m (the scripted driver finishes in 30.17 s). The clip replays this run.
caption.Over many runs: in 200 runs each on this track, random actions are out after 9.4 s on average (median 6.1 s, 10–90 % range 2.0–21.0 s) and the untrained network with sampled actions after 9.8 s (median 6.5 s, 2.0–23.1 s), with no detectable difference between them (Mann–Whitney p = 0.50 for the time, 0.48 for the progress). The gap between the two random clips is therefore consistent with luck, and this run is a lucky one, above the 90th percentile of its runs (`results/demos/random-vs-sampled/campaign-01.json`, `scripts/14_random_vs_sampled.py`).

title: Random actions (control) on the specialist's track
explain: This control presses a uniformly random key combination every agent step (0.05 s). Gas, coast and brake, which reverses at a standstill, each come up a third of the time and cancel out, so the car makes almost no progress and is out under the "no 0.5 m of progress in 2 s" rule.

caption.What you see: This control presses a uniformly random key combination every agent step (0.05 s). Gas, coast and brake, which reverses at a standstill, each come up a third of the time and cancel out, so the car makes almost no progress and is out under the "no 0.5 m of progress in 2 s" rule.
caption.Model: `baselines/random/seed0`: random actions, a uniformly random key combination every agent step from a seeded generator (seed 0); no network and no training; a control.
caption.Map: First Flight (`campaign-01`), a hand-made campaign track, 628 m long with 1 jump and up to 6° of banking; random actions ignore the track entirely.
caption.Evaluation: official evaluation in `results/baselines/random/seed0/eval_campaign.csv` (standing start, most probable action, final checkpoint): did not finish: stalled after 2.00 s and 6 m (the scripted driver finishes in 30.17 s). The clip replays this run.
caption.Over many runs: in 200 runs each on this track, random actions are out after 9.4 s on average (median 6.1 s, 10–90 % range 2.0–21.0 s) and the untrained network with sampled actions after 9.8 s (median 6.5 s, 2.0–23.1 s), with no detectable difference between them (Mann–Whitney p = 0.50 for the time, 0.48 for the progress). The gap between the two random clips is therefore consistent with luck, and this run is an unlucky one: 27% of its runs end at 2.0 s like this one (`results/demos/random-vs-sampled/campaign-01.json`, `scripts/14_random_vs_sampled.py`).
